stories.headline: Islands fill up as summer heat settles in, and the city asks for a lighter touch on the tap
stories.dek: Visitors are packing Mustang and Padre islands this July. Back on the mainland, Corpus Christi's water utility is asking residents to conserve while the heat holds.
body: By 9 a.m. Thursday, the line of cars waiting for the Port Aransas ferry had already stretched back along the highway from Harbor Island, and the sand on Mustang Island was dotted with canopies from the jetties south. It is the heart of summer on the Coastal Bend, and the islands are full.
Rental houses, hotels and beach parking areas on Mustang and North Padre islands have been busy since school let out, and the heavy tourist traffic shows no sign of easing during the hot weeks ahead.

Back on the mainland, the heat is showing up somewhere else: on the water meter. The City of Corpus Christi's water utility is urging residents to conserve while temperatures stay high, asking them to stick to the city's watering schedule, water lawns early in the morning or late in the evening instead of midafternoon, and fix dripping faucets and running toilets.

"Summer is when demand climbs fastest, and a lot of that is lawns," said Teresa Gallegos, a spokesperson for the utility. "We're not asking anyone to suffer through the heat. We're asking people to water at the right time, fix the leak they've been meaning to fix, and think twice before they hose down the driveway."

The city's drinking water is treated at the O.N. Stevens Water Treatment Plant in Calallen, on the Nueces River at the city's northwest edge, before it is pumped across Corpus Christi and to neighboring communities.

Leticia Ramos, 45, a schoolteacher who lives in Calallen not far from the plant, said her street has gotten the message, mostly. "My tomatoes are on the schedule like everybody else's," Ramos said. "What I'd like is for the city to just text me when something changes, instead of me finding out from a neighbor's post three days later."
Gallegos said the utility posts conservation updates on the city's website and social media accounts and encouraged residents to sign up for city alerts.
For visitors, the heat brings its own reminders: drink water before you feel thirsty, find shade during the middle of the day, and respect the rip current flags at the beach.

stories.headline: Corpus Christi crude loadings run near record pace; offshore anchorage stays busy
stories.dek: Export terminals on the Corpus Christi Ship Channel are loading tankers at one of their fastest clips on record, and vessels waiting for berths remain a routine sight off Port Aransas.
body: Crude oil loadings at the Port of Corpus Christi are running at a near-record pace this summer. Export terminals along the ship channel are working a steady rotation of tankers, and inbound vessels routinely hold at the offshore anchorage east of Port Aransas until berths clear.

The pattern is familiar to anyone watching public AIS data off the Coastal Bend. Laden and ballast tankers alternate through the entrance channel between the Port Aransas jetties, take a pilot and transit the Corpus Christi Ship Channel to terminals at Ingleside and along the Inner Harbor. Vessels without a confirmed berth window anchor offshore and wait.

"Our terminals are busy, the channel is open and the ships keep coming," said Javier Salinas, a spokesperson for the Port of Corpus Christi. "Seeing tankers at the anchorage is a sign of demand. That's what a working export port looks like."

Anchorage time is driven by several factors: berth availability, cargo readiness at the terminal, pilot and tug scheduling, and the transit restrictions that apply to the largest ships in the channel. Depending on the queue, a tanker can wait hours or several days.
Crude reaches the terminals by pipeline from West Texas production fields. The export trade has reshaped the port, adding storage tanks, dock space and a deeper channel to handle larger ships.

The practical effect of the pace is tighter scheduling. With berths in steady use, a vessel that arrives late for its window, or a terminal that falls behind on cargo, can push the next ship back into the anchorage queue.

For mariners, the result is a busier pass. Ferries crossing to Port Aransas, recreational boats, offshore supply vessels and harbor tugs share the entrance with deep-draft tankers, and summer adds charter and pleasure traffic to the mix.
Gulfwater will continue to track anchorage conditions and channel traffic at Corpus Christi through the summer.

stories.headline: Islands are packed this weekend: what to know before you head to the beach
stories.dek: Heavy summer crowds are filling Mustang and Padre islands. Here is how to beat the lines and the heat.
body: The islands are full. Cars line up for the Port Aransas ferry before breakfast, and beach parking on Mustang and North Padre islands is filling fast this Saturday as summer crowds pour onto the coast.

If you are heading out, plan for heat and plan for waiting. Bring more water than you think you need. Pack shade. Check the ferry status before you leave, or take the JFK Causeway onto Padre Island and drive north on Highway 361 to reach Mustang Island from the south.

At Hargrove Bait & Tackle near the jetties in Port Aransas, owner Bill Hargrove has been opening early. "Busiest I've seen it in a while. Everybody wants shrimp, ice and directions, in that order," Hargrove says. "I only charge for two of those."
City water officials are also asking residents to go easy on the tap while the heat holds. Water lawns early or late, and only on your scheduled day.
Heat safety: Watch for dizziness, headache, nausea and confusion. Move anyone showing those signs into shade, cool them with water and call 911 if symptoms get worse or the person stops sweating.
Rip currents: Swim near lifeguards where they are on duty, and obey the beach flags. If a current pulls you out, do not fight it. Swim parallel to the shore until you are free, then swim back in.
Leave the dunes alone: Park only in marked or allowed areas, and keep vehicles off the dunes and out of soft sand you are not sure about.
Harborline 6 will update beach and traffic conditions through the weekend.

stories.headline: Where the river meets the bay: a summer morning in the Nueces Delta
stories.dek: At the head of Nueces Bay, the marshes of the Nueces Delta are humming with birds, crabbers and kayakers, a quieter side of a busy coastal summer.
body: At first light the water in the Nueces Delta is the color of strong tea and almost perfectly still. A great blue heron works the edge of a cordgrass bank. Somewhere out of sight, a mullet jumps twice. Across Nueces Bay, the refinery stacks along the ship channel catch the sun before anything else does.

This is the other Coastal Bend summer. While Mustang and Padre islands fill with beach crowds, the marshes where the Nueces River spreads into Nueces Bay draw a smaller set of regulars: kayakers who put in along the river near Calallen, families crabbing with chicken necks and string at the bay's edge, and birders with long lenses and longer patience.

The delta is a nursery. Young shrimp, crabs and fish shelter in its shallow channels and tidal creeks before moving out into the open bay, which is one reason the marshes matter to the shrimpers and anglers who work Nueces and Corpus Christi bays.

It is also a place shaped by people. The Nueces River runs past the city's water treatment plant at Calallen before it reaches the marsh, and in a hot summer, when the city is asking residents to conserve, the river slides through the delta slowly, almost lazily, toward the bay.

Paddlers who know the delta say mornings are the time to go. By noon the heat is heavy, the southeast wind picks up and the open bay chops into short, steep waves. Bring more water than seems reasonable, a hat, a charged phone in a dry bag and someone on shore who knows when you plan to be back.

On the way out, the Nueces Bay Causeway carries a steady line of traffic between Corpus Christi and Portland, and from the open bay the bridges and the industrial skyline beyond them look closer than they are. For a few hours in the early morning, though, the loudest thing in the delta is the birds.

stories.headline: Army depot is hiring helicopter mechanics, and it is looking close to home
stories.dek: Corpus Christi Army Depot, one of the region's biggest employers, is recruiting mechanics to repair and overhaul Army helicopters at its hangars on Naval Air Station Corpus Christi.
body: Most people in Corpus Christi have driven past the Army depot without ever seeing inside it. Behind the gates of Naval Air Station Corpus Christi, in hangars near the edge of the bay, civilian workers take Army helicopters apart down to the airframe, repair them and send them back to units around the world.
Now the depot is hiring helicopter mechanics, and it is pitching the jobs to local workers.

"We want people who like to fix things and want to do work that matters," said Brenda Kowalczyk, a public affairs specialist for Corpus Christi Army Depot. "A lot of our mechanics grew up here, learned the trade here and stayed. That's the workforce we're trying to keep building."

The depot is the Defense Department's primary facility for overhauling rotary-wing aircraft and their components, and its civilian workforce makes it one of the largest employers in the Coastal Bend. The work runs from airframe and sheet-metal repair to engines, rotor components and the wiring and electronics that tie them together.

The hangars are a long way from a typical shop floor. Mechanics work from detailed technical manuals, and every repair is documented and inspected before an aircraft or component moves to the next station. "It's precise work, and it's work you can be proud of," Kowalczyk said.

Kowalczyk said applicants with aviation maintenance training or military mechanic experience are a natural fit, and that the depot trains new hires on its own procedures and standards. "If you've turned a wrench in the military, at a refinery or on a shrimp boat, there's a place to start the conversation," she said.

For the regional economy, the hiring is one more sign of a busy summer. Next door on the air station, Navy training squadrons are flying a normal summer schedule, and along the ship channel, crude export terminals are loading tankers at a near-record pace.
Job seekers can find the depot's openings on USAJOBS, the federal government's hiring site, Kowalczyk said.

stories.headline: Summer in the pattern: student pilots keep NAS Corpus Christi busy
stories.dek: Training squadrons at Naval Air Station Corpus Christi are flying a normal summer schedule, and in Flour Bluff the sound of turboprops is part of the morning.
body: On a weekday morning in Flour Bluff, the first sound after the mockingbirds is usually a propeller. Training aircraft from Naval Air Station Corpus Christi climb out over the water, turn, and come back around, again and again, as student naval aviators work the landing pattern.

Summer is not a slow season at the air station. Its training squadrons are flying a normal summer schedule, according to the station's public affairs office, moving students through a syllabus that eventually sends them on to advanced training and the fleet.

"Summer is a normal training season for us," said Lt. Marcus Hale, a public affairs officer for NAS Corpus Christi. "Students are flying, instructors are flying, and the base is operating the way it's supposed to. If you live nearby, that's the sound you're hearing."

For listeners who do not work on base, it helps to know what shares that patch of land at the end of Ocean Drive, between Corpus Christi Bay and Oso Bay. NAS Corpus Christi is home to Navy flight training, and it hosts tenant commands that include Corpus Christi Army Depot, where civilian workers overhaul Army helicopters, and a Coast Guard air station. The depot is also hiring helicopter mechanics this summer.

Flight training works like a pipeline. Students arrive with classroom training behind them, learn to fly in the local pattern and over nearby outlying fields, and leave qualified for the next stage. The pace is steady by design, which is why the sound over Flour Bluff changes so little from week to week.

For anyone who has served, the rhythm is familiar. Training commands run on schedules built months in advance, and a normal summer schedule means the syllabus is moving as planned: students are progressing, aircraft are available and instructors are in the cockpit.

For the surrounding neighborhoods, the base is both a neighbor and an employer. Many families in Flour Bluff and on Padre Island include someone who works on the station, in uniform or as a civilian, and the morning traffic at the gates tracks the training day.
Hale said residents with questions about aircraft noise or base activity can contact the station's public affairs office. "We'd rather answer a question than have people guess," he said.

stories.headline: Corpus Christi crude loadings hold near-record pace as tankers queue offshore
stories.dek: The Texas export hub keeps its berths full through July; analysts say anchorage waits reflect steady demand rather than disruption.
body: CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Sabal Energy Wire) — Crude loadings at the Port of Corpus Christi are running near record pace this summer, with export terminals working a full rotation of tankers and inbound vessels routinely waiting at the offshore anchorage east of Port Aransas before berthing.

The port's export docks draw crude by pipeline from the Permian Basin, and terminal operators have kept loading schedules tight through July. Anchorage waits have become a standing feature of the trade rather than a sign of trouble, market participants said.

"Corpus is where the Permian meets the water," said Grace Holloway, an energy market analyst at Lanternfish Energy Analytics. "When you see tankers lined up offshore, that's the market telling you the barrels are moving. The question traders ask isn't whether the docks are busy. It's whether anything slows them down."

Holloway said the steady pace gives buyers confidence in Gulf Coast supply, but that a hub running this efficiently has little room to absorb an interruption. "The flip side of being this efficient is that there isn't much slack," she said. "If something pauses loadings here, freight schedules feel it fast."

Market participants said Corpus Christi's role has grown alongside Permian production, with each new pipeline and dock expansion pulling more export volume to the Coastal Bend rather than to other Gulf ports.
For shipowners, the steady loading program has kept tankers positioned in the western Gulf, and charterers are watching berth availability closely as the summer wears on.
A port spokesperson has described the anchorage traffic as a normal part of a busy export season.
Sabal Energy Wire tracks Gulf Coast crude export flows weekly.

stories.headline: From a North Beach lawn chair, a retired welder watches the export boom sail by
stories.dek: Marcus Bell spent his working life welding along the ship channel. Now he watches the tankers it serves from a lawn chair on North Beach.
body: Marcus Bell does not need a ship-tracking app. From the lawn chair outside his place on North Beach, the 67-year-old retired welder can watch the tankers slide past between the beach and downtown, close enough to hear the engines, headed for the docks of the Inner Harbor or back out toward the Gulf.
"Used to be a big ship came under that bridge and people would stop what they were doing and watch," Bell said. "Now there's one coming or going all day long, and nobody looks up but me."

He has reason to look. Bell spent more than 30 years welding pipe and steel at refineries and fabrication yards along the Corpus Christi Ship Channel, and he still talks about the waterfront the way some people talk about an old job site: by who built what, and how well.

The traffic he watches is part of a boom. Crude export terminals at the Port of Corpus Christi are loading tankers at a near-record pace this summer, and vessels waiting for a berth routinely sit at the offshore anchorage east of Port Aransas. Crude arrives by pipeline from West Texas and leaves by ship, and the channel past North Beach is one of the routes it takes.
Summer brings its own traffic to North Beach: families on the sand, visitors at the aquarium and the aircraft carrier museum, and weekend cars backing up on the Harbor Bridge.

Bell keeps an eye on that, too. North Beach sits on a narrow strip of land between Corpus Christi Bay and Nueces Bay, and the way in and out runs over bridges: the Harbor Bridge to downtown and the Nueces Bay Causeway toward Portland. "You live out here, you learn the bridge is your front door," he said.

Asked what he thinks about when the tankers pass, Bell shrugged. "Steel and welds," he said. "Every one of those ships is somebody's good work or somebody's shortcut. You can't tell which from a lawn chair."

stories.headline: At hurricane fair, county's message to residents without cars: tell us now
stories.dek: Nueces County emergency managers handed out flashlights, evacuation maps and a plea Wednesday: if you will need a ride out in a storm, register before one is on the way.
body: Rosa Elizondo came to the hurricane fair for the free flashlight. Her youngest, 6, came for the bubbles. By the time they left a recreation center gym Wednesday afternoon, Elizondo, 38, also had a registration card for evacuation help folded into her purse.
"I don't have a car. I have three kids and two bus routes," said Elizondo, a home health aide who rents a few blocks from the bay. "If they tell us to leave, I need somebody to tell me how."

That is exactly the conversation Nueces County emergency managers say they want to have now, long before any storm. At hurricane-season preparedness fairs this summer, county staff are walking residents through evacuation zones and go-kits and urging anyone without a vehicle to register for evacuation assistance.

"If you don't have a way out, we need to know who you are and where you are before the storm, not during it," said Dwayne Pruitt, public information officer for the Nueces County Office of Emergency Management. "Once the wind picks up, it's too late to start a list."

Residents can sign up through the state's emergency assistance registry by dialing 2-1-1, Pruitt said. The registry is for anyone who would need help in an evacuation, including people without transportation, not only people with disabilities or medical needs.
Tables around the gym offered evacuation-zone maps, battery radios, first-aid checklists and advice on storing documents in waterproof bags. Children collected stickers. Adults collected paperwork.

Pastor Gloria Whitfield, 59, brought a carload of neighbors from her church and stood in line with them. She keeps her own list of who on her streets has no car or no phone, she said, and she wants the county's list to match. "I know who those people are by name," Whitfield said. "The county should too. A list in my notebook doesn't send a bus."
Elizondo said she would fill out the card that night, after the kids were asleep. "If I don't fall asleep first," she said, laughing. "Ay, Dios. Ask me in a week."

stories.headline: Hurricane season starts at the kitchen table: a checklist for base families
stories.dek: County preparedness fairs are open to everyone, including military households. Here is what to do now, plus news from the depot's hiring push.
body: If your family moved to the Coastal Bend this year, welcome. You picked a beautiful place, and you arrived in hurricane season. The good news is that most of the work of getting ready happens at your own kitchen table, long before anyone is watching a forecast.

Nueces County emergency managers are holding hurricane-season preparedness fairs this summer, and military families are welcome. The county's message is simple: know your evacuation zone, build a kit, and if you will not have a vehicle, register for evacuation help now through the state's 2-1-1 registry.

"Military families are our neighbors, and the same advice applies: know your zone and have a plan to leave," said Dwayne Pruitt, public information officer for the Nueces County Office of Emergency Management. "If you won't have a car, tell us now, not when the wind is blowing."

That last point matters more than many families expect. A household with one car and a spouse away on duty can find itself without a ride on the day it counts. Make a plan with a neighbor, a friend from your command's family readiness group, or the county registry.

Your kitchen-table checklist: Look up your evacuation zone and save it in your phone. Keep copies of orders, IDs, insurance papers and medical records in a waterproof bag. Stock water, nonperishable food, medications, chargers and pet supplies. Know how your command will account for you and how to check in if you leave the area. Pick a meeting place and an out-of-town contact.

Depot hiring: Corpus Christi Army Depot is recruiting helicopter mechanics. "Veterans and military spouses bring exactly the kind of discipline this work needs," said Brenda Kowalczyk, a depot public affairs specialist. Openings are posted on USAJOBS.
Flight line: Training squadrons at NAS Corpus Christi are flying a normal summer schedule, so expect the usual sound of turboprops over Flour Bluff.

stories.headline: Fact check: Evacuation help is not just for people with disabilities. No car? Sign up.
stories.dek: Some residents believe the state's evacuation assistance registry is only for people with medical needs. County emergency managers say anyone who would need a ride should register.
body: The claim: Harborline 6 viewers have told us they skipped signing up for evacuation help because they heard the registry is "only for people in wheelchairs" or "only for people on oxygen."
The verdict: False. Nueces County emergency managers are urging residents who do not have a car to register for evacuation assistance, whether or not they have a disability or a medical need.

"If you don't have a way to leave, you're who this is for," says Dwayne Pruitt, public information officer for the Nueces County Office of Emergency Management. "Don't talk yourself out of it. Let us figure out what help you need."

The county has been making that pitch at hurricane-season preparedness fairs this summer. At one Wednesday, as the Bayside Ledger reported, staff handed registration cards to families who get around by bus.

How to sign up: Dial 2-1-1 and ask to join the state's emergency assistance registry. You will be asked for your address, how many people live with you and what kind of help you would need. A relative, neighbor or church volunteer can help you register.

What it is not: Registering does not guarantee a ride at a specific time, so it should not replace your own plan. Know your evacuation zone, keep a go-bag ready and line up a neighbor or relative who can drive you if possible.
Why it matters: Emergency planners use the registry to understand who in their community may need help and what kind. If people who need a ride are not on it, planners cannot count them.
Bottom line: If you will not have a car when an evacuation order comes, sign up now.

stories.headline: In summer heat, home health aides keep watch over the people most at risk
stories.dek: Older and homebound residents are among the most vulnerable in a Coastal Bend summer. The aides who visit them are often the first to notice trouble.
body: Rosa Elizondo starts every visit the same way. Before she checks a pill organizer or helps a client to the shower, she walks to the thermostat and looks at the number.

"If the house is hot, everything else waits," said Elizondo, 38, a home health aide who rides city buses between clients' homes across Corpus Christi. "Some of my ladies won't turn on the air because of the bill. I tell them, señora, the light bill is cheaper than the hospital."

The heat that is filling Mustang and Padre islands with beachgoers this summer is a different problem indoors. Older adults, people with heart or lung disease and people who take certain medications can overheat without feeling especially thirsty, and a house without working air conditioning can become dangerous over a few days.

Elizondo, a mother of three who does not own a car, spends part of each workday waiting at bus stops in the same heat. She carries two frozen water bottles in her bag, one for herself and one for whichever client needs it more. "By the second bus it's just cold water," she said. "By the third client it's warm water. Still water."

What to watch for: Heat exhaustion can bring heavy sweating, weakness, dizziness, headache, nausea or muscle cramps. Heat stroke is an emergency, marked by confusion, a very high body temperature and hot skin. Call 911 for anyone with signs of heat stroke, and cool them with water and shade while you wait.

What to do: Check on older neighbors at least once a day during hot spells. Make sure fans and air conditioners work, close blinds in the afternoon and offer water often. If someone cannot keep a home cool, help them spend the hottest hours somewhere air-conditioned, such as a library or a store.

Elizondo said the hardest part of the job in July is not the work itself. "It's leaving," she said. "You lock the door and you think, is she going to be OK tonight? So I call. Everybody gets a phone call before I go to bed."

stories.headline: Bay shrimpers see a fair start to the season, but diesel is eating the margin
stories.dek: In Aransas Pass, shrimpers say catches have been decent so far. The trouble is what it costs to go out and get them.
body: The shrimp boats at Aransas Pass leave the harbor before the sun is fully up, outriggers raised like folded wings, and come back in the afternoon heat with gulls trailing behind them. So far this season, the boats have had something to show for it.
Bay shrimpers describe a fair start to the season, with steady catches in the bays around Aransas Pass. What they do not describe as fair is the fuel bill.

"The shrimp are there. That's not the problem," said Huy Nguyen, 51, who owns a shrimp boat out of Aransas Pass. "Diesel is the problem. Fuel is the first bill and the biggest one. You pay it before you know if you caught anything."

Nguyen learned the bays on his father's boat and has worked them most of his life. He talks about the business in plain arithmetic: a good day pays for the fuel, the ice and the deckhand, and maybe a little toward what he owes on the boat. A slow day does not. "Three good days and one bad one, you're even," he said. "Two bad ones, you're borrowing."
The squeeze is familiar along the Texas coast, where small family operations compete with imported shrimp on price and absorb swings in fuel, ice and repair costs on thin margins.
At the docks, the routine is the same whether the day was good or bad: hose the deck, ice what came in, settle up with the buyer and look at the fuel gauge. Nguyen does the last part twice.

The bays themselves look healthy to the people who work them. Nguyen said the shrimp have been running at a decent size this summer, and the grass flats where young shrimp grow have looked good on the clear days. "The bay is doing its part," he said. "I'm trying to do mine."
Asked what would make the season, he did not hesitate. "Cheaper fuel and no surprises," Nguyen said. "On the water, surprises are never the good kind."

stories.headline: The pastor who keeps a list
stories.dek: Pastor Gloria Whitfield knows which neighbors have no car, which have no phone and which can't manage stairs. She wants the county to know too.
body: The notebook lives in Pastor Gloria Whitfield's purse, a spiral-bound thing with a cracked cover and a rubber band around it. Inside, in pencil, are names and street addresses, and next to them a shorthand only she fully understands: "no car," "no phone," "walker," "son in Houston," "will need help with the dog."
"This is my parish," said Whitfield, 59, tapping the cover. "Not the building. The people in this book."

Whitfield runs meals and supplies out of her church's fellowship hall in a low-income neighborhood near the bay, where many households do not have a vehicle and some do not have a working phone. On Wednesdays the hall smells like rice, beans and coffee. On any other day, she said, the door opens if someone needs it to.

As the Ledger reported Wednesday, she brought a carload of neighbors to a Nueces County hurricane-season preparedness fair, where emergency managers urged residents without cars to register for evacuation assistance. Whitfield stood in line with them while they filled out cards.

"I'm not against the county. I'm for the county knowing what I know," she said. "When they tell people to leave, the people in this book can't just leave. Somebody has to come. And somebody has to know where to come."

Her list started years ago as a prayer list and grew into something more practical: who needs groceries carried in, who needs a ride to the doctor, who has grandchildren staying for the summer. She updates it after every service and every meal.

Neighbors say the list works because of who keeps it. "She knows before I tell her," said Rosa Elizondo, 38, a home health aide and mother of three who relies on buses. "That's Pastor Gloria. You don't call her. She calls you."

Whitfield said her goal for the summer is simple: every person in her notebook who would need a ride out of a storm should be on the county's registry as well. "I'll sit at the kitchen table with them and dial the phone myself," she said. "God gave me a car and a loud voice. I intend to use both."

stories.headline: NAS Corpus Christi completes routine readiness inspection; base services normal
stories.dek: The air station says a scheduled inspection has wrapped up with no change to day-to-day services for service members, civilian workers or families.
body: Naval Air Station Corpus Christi has completed a routine readiness inspection, and base services are operating normally, the station's public affairs office said Monday.

"This was a scheduled inspection, the kind every installation goes through, and it's complete," said Lt. Marcus Hale, a public affairs officer for NAS Corpus Christi. "The gates, the clinic, the commissary and the flight line are all running normal hours. Families shouldn't notice anything different."

For people outside the military, the word "inspection" can sound like trouble. It usually is not. Installations and commands are inspected on a regular cycle to make sure equipment, facilities, training and emergency plans meet Navy standards, and the detailed results generally stay inside the chain of command. The station did not release results, which is typical.

Preparing for an inspection usually means weeks of extra work: checking maintenance logs, updating emergency plans, inventorying equipment and making sure training records are current. For the people who do that work, the end of an inspection mostly means getting back to the regular job.

The air station hosts Navy flight training squadrons, which have been flying a normal summer schedule, along with tenant commands that include Corpus Christi Army Depot and a Coast Guard air station. The depot has been hiring helicopter mechanics this summer.

For the Flour Bluff and Padre Island neighborhoods around the base, the practical meaning of Monday's announcement is that nothing changes. The morning training flights continue, the gates keep their usual hours and the people who work on the station keep their routines.
That routine is a big part of life on this end of the city. Base employees fill the lunch spots along the main roads into the station, and the training schedule sets the rhythm of the sky overhead.
For military families, the bigger summer news on base has been more ordinary: moving season, with new arrivals reporting in and others packing for their next assignment.
Hale said questions about base services can go to the station's public affairs office. Coastline Public Radio covers the Coastal Bend's military installations and the families connected to them.

stories.headline: Explainer: how the Corpus Christi offshore anchorage works when the docks are full
stories.dek: Tankers waiting off Port Aransas are a routine part of a near-record export summer. Here is how the queue is managed.
body: With crude export terminals on the Corpus Christi Ship Channel loading at a near-record pace, the offshore anchorage east of Port Aransas has become a fixture on public vessel-tracking screens. On a typical day, tankers swing at anchor in the open Gulf, waiting for a berth.

Anchoring: Vessels that arrive without an open berth anchor in designated areas outside the entrance channel. Position, weather and holding ground all matter. In a strong onshore wind, masters may choose to drift or steam offshore rather than ride at anchor.

Sequencing: Terminals, ship agents and the port coordinate berth windows. When a berth clears, the next vessel is called in, picks up a pilot outside the jetties and transits the channel with tug assistance as required. The largest tankers face transit limits based on draft, beam, visibility and wind.
Why ships wait: Cargo readiness at the terminal, shore tank levels, documentation and inspections, and the departure of the vessel ahead all affect timing. Waits range from hours to days.

Who manages it: The Coast Guard sets port conditions and oversees traffic in the channel. Pilots, terminal operators and agents handle day-to-day movements. The port authority, which owns much of the dock infrastructure, describes the anchorage traffic as a normal sign of demand, as a port spokesperson told Gulfwater this month.

Mixed traffic: The anchorage area is also used by product tankers, bulk carriers and offshore supply vessels, and it sits near the approaches used by fishing and charter boats out of Port Aransas. AIS gives a reasonable picture of the larger ships present, although small craft are not required to broadcast and often do not.
Gulfwater will continue to report anchorage and channel conditions at Corpus Christi through the summer.

stories.headline: Fort Hood aviation brigade to ship helicopters through Port of Corpus Christi in late summer
stories.dek: The brigade's helicopters and equipment will move through the port on the way to an overseas rotation, Army and port officials said Wednesday.
body: An Army aviation brigade from Fort Hood will move its helicopters and equipment through the Port of Corpus Christi in late summer on the way to an overseas rotation, Army and port officials said Wednesday.

"Our soldiers are trained and ready, and our equipment will be too," said Maj. Darnell Price, a public affairs officer at Fort Hood. "We'll be ready to deploy when the port is ready for us, and the Port of Corpus Christi has been a reliable partner in getting Army equipment where it needs to go."
Price did not give a date or a destination beyond describing the movement as an overseas rotation, which is standard practice for unit movements.

Rotations like this one separate people from equipment. Soldiers typically fly. A brigade's helicopters, vehicles and containers travel by road and rail to a port, where they are inspected, staged and loaded aboard a sealift ship. Helicopters are usually prepared for the voyage with rotor blades folded or removed and protective wrapping against salt air.
Corpus Christi is a natural choice. The port is one of the Defense Department's designated strategic seaports, and it has handled Army deployments before.

For the port, a brigade movement is a familiar if infrequent job. Military equipment is handled at general cargo docks rather than at the crude terminals that dominate the channel, where tankers have been loading at a near-record pace this summer. Staging can take days, as equipment arrives, is checked against load plans and is positioned for loading.

"This is a community that's proud of its military connections, and the port is proud of this role," said Javier Salinas, a spokesperson for the Port of Corpus Christi. "We'll work the military cargo alongside our regular business. Our people know how to do both."

For residents, the most visible part of a brigade move is usually the staging at the docks rather than anything on the water. The Army has not released details of how or when equipment will arrive in Corpus Christi, and Coastline Public Radio does not report unit movement details before public affairs officials release them.
Families with questions about the rotation should get information through their soldier's unit and its family readiness group.

stories.headline: Why the Army ships helicopters out of Corpus Christi, and how that fits with the oil trade
stories.dek: A Fort Hood aviation brigade's late-summer movement will share a busy ship channel with near-record crude exports. Here is how the port handles both.
body: The Port of Corpus Christi is best known these days for oil. Crude export terminals along the ship channel are loading tankers at a near-record pace, and ships waiting for a berth are a routine sight at the anchorage off Port Aransas.

But the port has a second job that gets less attention until a moment like this one. On Wednesday, Army and port officials said an aviation brigade from Fort Hood will move its helicopters and equipment through Corpus Christi in late summer on the way to an overseas rotation.

Why here: The port is one of a small group of commercial ports the Defense Department has designated as strategic seaports, meaning it has agreed to make dock space and services available for military cargo when needed. It sits a few hours' drive from Fort Hood, has deep water and has handled Army cargo before.

How it fits: Military equipment does not load at the crude docks. Helicopters, vehicles and containers move through general cargo berths that can handle roll-on, roll-off ships, where equipment is driven or towed aboard. That keeps the brigade's loading physically apart from the tanker traffic, though both share the same channel, and the same pilots and tugs, to reach the Gulf.
"Scheduling is what we do every day," said Javier Salinas, a spokesperson for the port. "Tankers, cargo ships, military moves. Everybody gets a slot, and everybody gets out on time."

The economics: A single military move is a small piece of the port's business compared with the daily crude trade. But it brings work for longshore crews, truck drivers, security staff and port employees during staging and loading, and it reinforces a relationship with the Army that the port counts as part of its identity.
What is not public: The Army has not released dates, routes or the number of aircraft involved, and officials described the destination only as an overseas rotation.

stories.headline: This week on base: inspection wrapped, services normal, and a brigade headed for the port
stories.dek: NAS Corpus Christi finished a routine readiness inspection with no change to services, and a Fort Hood aviation brigade will move equipment through the Port of Corpus Christi in late summer.
body: A quick look at what is new around the installations this week.

Inspection complete: NAS Corpus Christi wrapped up a routine readiness inspection, and base services are operating normally. "Thank you to every sailor, civilian and contractor who put in the extra hours to get ready for it," said Lt. Marcus Hale, a station public affairs officer. "For families, nothing changes. Everything's open on its usual hours."

Brigade movement: An aviation brigade from Fort Hood will move its helicopters and equipment through the Port of Corpus Christi in late summer for an overseas rotation. "We'll be ready to deploy when the port is ready for us," Maj. Darnell Price, a Fort Hood public affairs officer, said in announcing the move Wednesday.

What that means locally: The move runs through the port, not the air station, and the Army has not released dates or details. As always, Anchor & Rotor does not report unit movement details beyond what public affairs offices release. If you have a loved one in the brigade, your soldier's unit and family readiness group are the right sources for information.
Depot still hiring: Corpus Christi Army Depot continues to recruit helicopter mechanics. Veterans and military spouses with maintenance experience can find openings on USAJOBS.
Flight line: Training squadrons are flying their normal summer schedule. Expect turboprops over Flour Bluff on weekday mornings.

Hurricane season reminder: Nueces County preparedness fairs continue this summer. If your household will not have a car in an evacuation, register through the state registry by dialing 2-1-1, and make sure your command knows how to reach you if you leave town.
Have news from your squadron, shop or family group? Send it our way for a future issue.

stories.headline: Army outload to slot into Corpus Christi's crowded tanker schedule
stories.dek: A late-summer military movement will need berth time, pilots and tugs in a channel already running near-record crude volumes.
body: The Port of Corpus Christi will handle a Fort Hood aviation brigade's helicopters and equipment in late summer, Army and port officials said this week, adding a military outload to a channel already busy with near-record crude loadings.

Berths: Military equipment typically moves over general cargo or roll-on, roll-off berths rather than liquid bulk docks, so the outload does not compete directly with crude terminals for dock space. It does compete for channel time, pilots, tugs and line handlers.

Vessel: Unit equipment for overseas rotations commonly moves on government-controlled sealift ships with stern ramps and large internal vehicle decks. The Army has not identified the ship or released loading dates.

Staging: Before loading, unit equipment is typically marshaled in a staging area near the berth, checked against load plans and inspected for shipment. Helicopters usually move aboard with blades folded or removed and are secured on internal decks for the voyage.

Channel: Deep-draft tankers dominate traffic between the Port Aransas jetties and the Inner Harbor. A sealift transit is one more large-ship movement to sequence, with the additional coordination typical of military cargo.

Anchorage: Inbound tankers already wait offshore for berth windows. A port spokesperson said this month that anchorage traffic reflects demand. A single military movement is unlikely to change that picture much, but scheduling margins in a peak export summer are thin.

Strategic seaport: Corpus Christi is one of the commercial ports designated by the Defense Department to support military deployments, and it has moved Army cargo before. "We'll work the military cargo alongside our regular business," port spokesperson Javier Salinas said Wednesday.
Outlook: As with any late-summer schedule on the Texas coast, weather is the main variable. Gulfwater will report channel conditions and the outload as details become public.

stories.headline: Why the city keeps asking you to save water in the summer
stories.dek: Every tap in Corpus Christi traces back to one treatment plant in Calallen. Here is how the water gets to you, and why the heat matters.
body: Turn on a faucet anywhere in Corpus Christi and the water coming out has made a long trip. It starts in reservoirs and the Nueces River, passes through the O.N. Stevens Water Treatment Plant in Calallen and travels through miles of pipe and pump stations before it reaches your kitchen.
That is why, when summer heat settles over the Coastal Bend, the city's water utility asks residents to conserve. It has been making that request again this month.

"Our system is built to meet demand, but summer stretches every part of it at once," said Teresa Gallegos, a spokesperson for the city's water utility. "When everyone waters at 4 in the afternoon, we're treating and pumping water that mostly evaporates. Shift it to early morning, fix the leak, and you're helping the whole system."

The basics: O.N. Stevens is the city's only water treatment plant. It draws raw water, treats and filters it, disinfects it and sends it out to homes, businesses and neighboring communities. Demand climbs in hot, dry weather, largely because of outdoor watering.

What you can do: Water lawns only on your scheduled day, and early or late. Use a broom, not a hose, on driveways. Run dishwashers and washing machines with full loads. Check for leaks; a running toilet can waste a surprising amount of water. Keep a pitcher of cold water in the refrigerator instead of running the tap until it cools.
A health note: Conserving water should never mean skimping on drinking water in the heat. Older adults, children and outdoor workers need to drink regularly, even if they do not feel thirsty.

Leticia Ramos, 45, a schoolteacher who lives in Calallen a few minutes from the plant, said neighbors take the conservation requests seriously but want clearer updates. "People out here will do their part," Ramos said. "We just want to hear it from the city first, in plain words, not from a rumor at the gas station."
The utility posts updates on the city's website and social media, Gallegos said, and residents can report leaks and water main breaks to the city.

stories.headline: No car, no easy way out: bus gaps shape life, and storm plans, in neighborhoods near the bay
stories.dek: Many households in Corpus Christi's low-income neighborhoods near the bay don't own a vehicle. Advocates say evacuation plans have to start with that fact.
body: At 6:10 on a weekday morning, the bus shelter near Rosa Elizondo's rented duplex is already warm. She has made the trip so many times she can tell the time by the light on the bay: first bus, a transfer downtown, a second bus, then a walk to her first client's door.

"If I miss one bus, my whole day moves," said Elizondo, 38, a home health aide and mother of three. "If the bus is late, I'm late. If my kid is sick, I'm counting bus times in my head before I'm counting fevers."

For many households in the low-income neighborhoods near the bay, life is organized around a bus schedule. Census data show these neighborhoods have some of the highest shares of households without a vehicle in the city, and service that works for a weekday commute can leave long gaps at night, on weekends and across town.

Advocates say those gaps matter most when the question is not how to get to work but how to get out. Nueces County emergency managers have been urging residents without cars to register for evacuation assistance at preparedness fairs this summer. Advocates want more: more pickup points, more rides and more outreach door to door.

"A plan that starts with 'get in your car' isn't a plan for my street," said Pastor Gloria Whitfield, 59, who runs a relief hub from her church's fellowship hall. "A lot of the people I feed on Wednesdays have never owned a car. They need a ride, and they need someone to knock on the door and tell them the ride is coming."

The county's registry is a start, Whitfield said, but it depends on people knowing about it, having a phone to call and trusting the system enough to use it. She has been sitting with neighbors to help them sign up.

Elizondo said she thinks about storms the way she thinks about buses: in terms of what happens if one thing goes wrong. "Everybody says, 'Just leave.' OK. In what?" she said, then laughed. "My neighbor's truck? The pastor's car? I'll take whatever's going. Pero somebody has to be going."
Coastline Public Radio is mapping transportation access across the Coastal Bend this hurricane season. If you live without a car and want to share how you would evacuate, contact our newsroom.

stories.headline: Advocates push for more evacuation rides for families without cars
stories.dek: Neighborhood leaders near the bay say a registry is not enough. Here is how to sign up for evacuation help now.
body: In neighborhoods near the bay, a lot of families do not have a car. Advocates say that has to change how Corpus Christi plans for a storm.

Pastor Gloria Whitfield runs a relief hub out of her church's fellowship hall. She says bus gaps already leave many of her neighbors stuck at night and on weekends, and an evacuation would be harder still. "Registering is step one," Whitfield tells Harborline 6. "Step two is somebody actually showing up. I want to see more rides, more pickup spots and people knocking on doors."

Nueces County emergency managers are urging residents without cars to register for evacuation help now, before any storm. "If you don't have a way out, tell us now," says Dwayne Pruitt, the public information officer for the county's emergency management office. "That's how we know where to send help."

How to register: Dial 2-1-1 and ask for the state's emergency assistance registry. You can register yourself or help a neighbor do it. It is not only for people with disabilities. If you will not have a ride, it is for you.

Make a backup plan: Ask a neighbor, relative or church member with a car whether they can take you. Write their number down on paper, not just in your phone. Keep a bag packed with medicines, documents and phone chargers.
Know your zone: Look up your evacuation zone on the county's website, or ask at one of the county's preparedness fairs this summer.
Harborline 6 will keep following the push for more evacuation rides.

stories.headline: Opinion: A ride out of a storm shouldn't depend on who you know
stories.dek: Nueces County asks residents without cars to register for evacuation help. That is necessary, and it is not enough.
body: Editor's note: This is an opinion column.
Every hurricane season, the advice arrives in the same shape: know your zone, pack a kit, fill the tank. For many families in this city, the last part does not apply. There is no tank to fill.

Nueces County emergency managers have been doing the right thing this summer. At preparedness fairs, they have urged residents without cars to register for evacuation assistance through the state's 2-1-1 registry, and they have said plainly that the registry is not only for people with disabilities. Last month I watched Rosa Elizondo, a home health aide and mother of three, fold a registration card into her purse at one of those fairs.

But registration is a list, and a list is only as good as the ride at the end of it. As Coastline Public Radio reported Saturday, advocates in neighborhoods near the bay say bus gaps already leave families stranded on ordinary weekends. Pastor Gloria Whitfield, who keeps her own notebook of neighbors without cars or phones, put it best: a list in a notebook doesn't send a bus.

Here is what the county and city could do before the season peaks. Publish where evacuation pickup points will be, neighborhood by neighborhood, now and not on the day of an order. Partner with churches and neighborhood hubs that already know who needs help. And go door to door in the neighborhoods where the fewest people own cars, rather than waiting for phone calls that may never come.

None of this is a criticism of the people who will drive the buses and staff the shelters. They have done this before, and they will do it again. It is a question of where the work starts. If the plan starts at the shelter door, it is already too late for the person who never made it to the bus.
A storm will not check who owns a car. Our plans shouldn't either.

stories.headline: Two ways off North Beach: summer crowds test the Harbor Bridge and the causeway
stories.dek: Heavy summer traffic is backing up the routes in and out of North Beach on weekends. Residents say the bridges are their lifeline.
body: Summer weekends on North Beach end the same way: a slow crawl toward the Harbor Bridge. Visitors leave the sand, the aquarium and the museum ship at about the same time, and the line of cars stretches back along the beach road.

North Beach sits on a narrow strip of land between Corpus Christi Bay and Nueces Bay. There are two ways off by car: the Harbor Bridge south to downtown, and the Nueces Bay Causeway north toward Portland. When one backs up, the other fills.

Marcus Bell, 67, has lived on North Beach long enough to plan his errands around it. "Saturday and Sunday, I don't go anywhere after lunch," says Bell, a retired welder. "You go over that bridge at 4 o'clock, you'd better have a full tank and a good radio station."

Tips for summer weekends: Head home before late afternoon if you can. Check traffic before you leave the beach. Keep water in the car, because idling in the sun gets hot fast. Watch your gas gauge, since both routes include long stretches of bridge with nowhere to pull off.
If you break down on a bridge, stay in your vehicle with your seat belt on, turn on your hazard lights and call 911.

Bell says the beach traffic is the price of living somewhere people want to visit. "I'll take it. It's pretty out here," he says. "But you learn real quick, out here the bridge isn't just a road. It's the door."
Harborline 6 posts weekend traffic updates for the Harbor Bridge, the Nueces Bay Causeway and the JFK Causeway on our Traffic page.

stories.headline: In Aransas Pass, a second-generation shrimper reads the bay and the fuel gauge
stories.dek: Huy Nguyen has worked the bays of the Coastal Bend most of his life. This summer's catch has been fair. The math has not.
body: Huy Nguyen keeps two kinds of records. One is in his head: where the shrimp were running last week, how the water looked, which way the wind will turn by afternoon. The other is a stack of fuel receipts clipped to the visor of his truck.
"The first one tells me where to go," said Nguyen, 51, who owns a shrimp boat out of Aransas Pass. "The second one tells me if I can afford to go."

Bay shrimpers describe a fair start to the season, and Nguyen agrees. But fuel costs have squeezed margins for small operators all summer, and boats that look busy from the harbor are often working for very thin returns.

Nguyen is a second-generation shrimper. He learned the bays on his father's boat, and he still talks about the water the way his father taught him to: as something alive that changes by the hour. The shallow marshes and seagrass beds that ring the bays are nurseries for young shrimp, crabs and fish, and the health of those habitats shows up, eventually, in his nets.

Mornings at the Aransas Pass docks start in the dark. Deckhands load ice and check the nets and winches, and the boats file out past the harbor markers before the heat sets in. By afternoon they are back, sorting the catch on deck while buyers wait on the dock.

"People think of the bay like a parking lot full of shrimp," he said. "It's not. It's a nursery. You take care of the nursery, the shrimp come. You mess up the nursery, you can have all the cheap fuel in the world and it doesn't matter."

For coastal towns like Aransas Pass, the shrimp fleet is part economy and part identity. Family operations depend on the bays, the docks, the ice houses and the buyers who take the catch, and a bad stretch for one tends to ripple through the others.

Nguyen said he has no plans to stop. His crew is small, his boat is old but sound, and the bays have been good to him more years than not. "I'm not complaining," he said, then reconsidered. "OK, I'm complaining about diesel. Not the bay. Never the bay."

stories.headline: A Calallen teacher's summer homework: a phone tree for her whole street
stories.dek: Leticia Ramos spent part of her summer break building a contact list for her neighbors. She says hurricane season is no time to wait for someone else to get organized.
body: Leticia Ramos has a clipboard, and she is not afraid to use it.

Over the past few weeks, the 45-year-old schoolteacher has knocked on nearly every door on her street in Calallen, on the northwest edge of Corpus Christi, collecting names, phone numbers and one more piece of information: who would need help if something went wrong.

"Teachers make lists. It's an occupational hazard," Ramos said from her kitchen table, where a printed spreadsheet sat next to a stack of classroom supplies she had bought for the fall. "I figured if we ever need to check on each other, I don't want to be standing in the street yelling names."

The idea came from a Nueces County hurricane-season preparedness fair, where emergency managers urged residents to make a plan and to register anyone without a car for evacuation assistance. Ramos left with a folder of handouts and a conviction that her street needed its own plan, too.

Her list notes which neighbors are older, who lives alone, who has a generator, who has a truck and who has young children. It also notes who does not have a smartphone, so they can be called rather than texted.

Ramos lives a few minutes from the O.N. Stevens Water Treatment Plant, and like her neighbors she follows the city's summer conservation requests closely. She has told the Ledger before that she wants the city to communicate faster and more plainly. "I'm not trying to replace anybody," she said. "I just think the fastest way to get news to my street is my street."
A few neighbors laughed at first, she said. Most have since asked for a copy. "Mrs. Ramos has a list" has become a running joke on the block, and something of a comfort.
"Nothing is happening," Ramos said. "That's exactly when you do this. You don't build the phone tree when the phone is already ringing."

stories.headline: Foreign government announces large naval and special-operations exercises far from the Gulf
stories.dek: Analysts describe the planned drills as a show of force and say they will watch the size and pace of the maneuvers closely.
body: WASHINGTON (Continental Wire) — A foreign government has announced large-scale naval and special-operations exercises far from the Gulf, a move defense analysts described as a show of force.

The announcement outlined drills involving naval forces and special-operations units. Analysts said the scale of the exercises, and the decision to publicize them in advance, suggested they were meant to be seen as much as to train forces.

Exercises of this kind are often aimed at more than one audience, analysts said: rival governments, neighboring states and a domestic public that the government wants to reassure about its military reach. Announcing large drills ahead of time is one of the more common ways governments send that message without a direct confrontation.

Naval exercises on this scale typically involve surface ships, submarines and aircraft rehearsing maneuvers at sea, sometimes far from home waters. Special-operations drills can include small-unit raids, ship boardings and maritime interdiction. Pairing the two, analysts said, is a way of signaling that a military can project force at a distance and act quickly once it arrives.

Governments that stage large exercises far from home must sustain ships and troops at a distance, with fuel, supplies and maintenance moving along long supply lines. Analysts said the logistics alone can reveal how prepared a military is to operate abroad for an extended period.
Such exercises are closely monitored by other navies and, increasingly, by commercial satellite imagery firms and independent researchers who track ship movements from open sources.

Analysts said they would watch for the actual size of the forces involved compared with what was announced, the duration of the drills, how close they come to other countries' forces and any change in the government's public tone while they are under way.

They also cautioned against reading too much into the announcement before the drills begin, noting that large, publicized exercises are a regular feature of many militaries' calendars and do not by themselves signal an intent to use force.

stories.headline: New to the Coastal Bend? Moving season meets hurricane season
stories.dek: Families arriving on summer orders have a lot to unpack. Put a hurricane plan near the top of the box pile.
body: Summer is moving season for military families, and the Coastal Bend is no exception. Moving trucks are pulling up to houses in Flour Bluff, Kingsville and Portland, and new arrivals are learning where the commissary is, which school their kids will attend and how hot August really gets.
There is one more thing to learn early: your hurricane plan.

Start with your county. Evacuation zones and orders come from local emergency managers, and they depend on where you live, not where you work. Families in Corpus Christi and Flour Bluff fall under Nueces County. Kingsville families should check with Kleberg County. Portland and Ingleside are in San Patricio County.

Nueces County has been holding preparedness fairs this summer and urging residents without cars to register for evacuation help through the state's 2-1-1 registry. "If you're new, come see us," said Dwayne Pruitt, public information officer for the Nueces County Office of Emergency Management. "Learn your zone before you need it, and learn it from us, not from the internet."

On base, it is business as usual. NAS Corpus Christi completed a routine readiness inspection last week, and services are running normally. "Everything's open. If you're new, come by and get your bearings," said Lt. Marcus Hale, a station public affairs officer.

New-arrival checklist: Save your county emergency office's website and social media accounts. Sign up for local alerts. Learn your evacuation zone. Keep orders, IDs and records in a waterproof bag. If your household has one car and a spouse who may be away, line up a backup ride now. Introduce yourself to a neighbor. And find your command's family readiness contacts before you need them.
Welcome to the Coastal Bend. The beaches are great, the people are friendly and the summer is long. Get your plan done early, and enjoy the rest.

stories.headline: What a "show of force" exercise is, and why analysts pay attention
stories.dek: A foreign government's announced naval and special-operations drills have drawn attention far from where they will take place. Here is how to read them.
body: When a foreign government announced large naval and special-operations exercises this week, analysts quickly reached for a familiar phrase: a show of force. For listeners in the Coastal Bend, where many families have someone in uniform, it is worth unpacking what that means, and what it does not.

Exercises are normal. Militaries train constantly, and big exercises are how they test whether ships, aircraft and units can work together under pressure. The U.S. military runs large exercises every year, often alongside allies.

Some exercises are meant to be seen. A "show of force" is an exercise whose audience is as much political as military. Announcing it publicly, holding it far from home and making it large are ways of telling other governments: we can operate here, at this scale. The drills announced this week were described as taking place far from the Gulf and involving both naval forces and special-operations units.

Special operations change the signal. Naval drills demonstrate reach. Adding special-operations forces, small units trained for raids, ship boardings and quiet work in contested places, suggests a government wants to show it can do more than sail ships in formation. That combination is one reason analysts are paying close attention.

What analysts watch next: the size of the forces actually involved compared with what was announced, whether the drills run longer than planned, how close they come to other countries' forces and what officials say while they are under way. An exercise that ends on schedule usually tells you one thing. One that keeps growing tells you another.

A note on language: officials and analysts often use "exercise," "drill" and "maneuvers" interchangeably. What matters more is scale, location and timing, which is why careful analysts wait for drills to begin before drawing conclusions.

Closer to home, the routine continues. Training squadrons at NAS Corpus Christi have been flying a normal summer schedule, and the air station said late last month that base services were operating normally after a routine inspection.
As any veteran will tell you, early reports from far away are often incomplete. Coastline Public Radio will follow the exercises as more becomes public, and will stick to what can be confirmed.

stories.headline: Port Aransas rides a strong summer: charters booked, bait shops busy
stories.dek: Businesses on Mustang Island say this has been a good season. Here is what to know if you are headed to Port Aransas this weekend.
body: Port Aransas is having a good summer. Charter boats are booked, the bait shops are busy and restaurants on the island have lines out the door on weekend nights.

Businesses on Mustang Island report a strong season, helped by steady crowds since early summer. At Hargrove Bait & Tackle near the jetties, owner Bill Hargrove says the shop has hardly had a quiet morning.
"I've had people waiting in the parking lot before I unlock the door," Hargrove says. "I asked one fella if he'd been there all night. He said, 'Not all night.'"
Anglers have been working the jetties, the surf and the bays, and kids are catching their first fish off the piers. Charter captains are running full trips on most weekends.

Headed over this weekend? Expect waits for the ferry at midday. Arriving early, or coming in from the south on the JFK Causeway and Highway 361, can help. Park only where it is allowed and check local beach rules before you drive on the sand.
Bring some cash for the smaller shops and bait stands, and be patient at the fuel docks and boat ramps, which are busiest early in the morning and again in the late afternoon.
Around the jetties, keep a close eye on kids. The rocks are slick and sharp, and big ships passing through the channel can push wakes onto the rocks without much warning.
Heat safety still applies. Take breaks in the shade, drink water and watch for signs of heat illness, including dizziness, headache and confusion.
Harborline 6 will be on the island this weekend. Send us your best catch photo.

stories.headline: Bait, ice and a few tall tales: Bill Hargrove's long view from the jetties
stories.dek: Bill Hargrove has sold bait near the Port Aransas jetties for decades. He has ridden out two hurricanes there, and he has opinions about almost everything else.
body: Bill Hargrove opens the shop before the gulls are fully awake. By 6 a.m. the aerators are bubbling in the live-bait tanks, the ice machine is groaning, and the first truck of the morning is idling in the shell lot outside Hargrove Bait & Tackle, a short walk from the Port Aransas jetties.
"Shrimp, ice, a weather report and a lie about where the reds are biting," said Hargrove, 64, ticking off his inventory. "Only one of those is free, and I won't tell you which."

Businesses in Port Aransas report a strong summer, with charters and bait shops busy, and Hargrove's register agrees. He has watched the island through good seasons and bad ones, and he can tell you which year the tarpon came back and which year the beach washed out, though the details shift a little depending on who is asking.

The jetties are his landmark and his living. Twin rock walls guard the pass where the Corpus Christi Ship Channel meets the Gulf, and every big ship headed to or from the port slides between them. Hargrove's customers fish the rocks while tankers pass close enough to feel through your feet. "Tourists take pictures of the ships," he said. "Locals take pictures of the fish. The ships don't care either way."
He knows the island's lore, too. He will tell you that a president once came to Port Aransas to fish for tarpon, and that the town was once called Tarpon, both of which happen to be true.

Hargrove has ridden out two hurricanes at the shop, including Harvey, which tore through Port Aransas and left much of the island in pieces. He does not romanticize it. "People think riding one out makes you tough. It makes you lucky," he said. "Everybody tells me I'm too old to do it again. Everybody's probably right."

For now, the worry is simpler: keeping enough bait in the tanks for a summer that won't slow down. "Good year," Hargrove said, sliding a bag of ice across the counter. "Knock on wood. Actually, knock on something sturdier than wood. This is Port A."

stories.headline: Summer scorecard: tankers, tourists and a depot that's hiring
stories.dek: From the export docks to the bait shops, the Coastal Bend economy has had a busy summer. A few soft spots are worth watching.
body: With August under way, the Coastal Bend's summer economy looks busy almost everywhere you check.

The port: Crude export terminals on the Corpus Christi Ship Channel have been loading tankers at a near-record pace all summer, and vessels waiting for berths have been a routine sight at the anchorage off Port Aransas. "The export machine is running about as hard as it can," said Grace Holloway, an energy market analyst at Lanternfish Energy Analytics. "That's good news for the region. Every tanker that loads is work for pilots, tug crews and line handlers."

The bases: Corpus Christi Army Depot is hiring helicopter mechanics, a steady source of skilled jobs, and training squadrons at NAS Corpus Christi have been flying a normal summer schedule. The air station completed a routine readiness inspection late last month with base services operating normally. A Fort Hood aviation brigade is scheduled to move its helicopters and equipment through the port in late summer, bringing short-term work for longshore crews and truck drivers.
The islands: Port Aransas businesses report a strong summer, with charters booked and bait shops busy. Mustang and Padre islands have drawn heavy crowds since early summer.

Soft spots: Bay shrimpers describe a fair start to the season, but fuel costs have squeezed margins. "Fuel is the first bill and the biggest one," Aransas Pass shrimper Huy Nguyen told the Ledger last month. And in low-income neighborhoods near the bay, transit gaps make it harder for households without cars to reach jobs across town, a cost that rarely shows up in economic statistics.

What to watch: Late summer is also the peak of hurricane season on the Gulf Coast. For a regional economy this tied to the water, a busy August can turn quickly on things no one controls, from weather to fuel prices to a single disruption in a crowded channel.
For now, the cash registers on the island, the paychecks at the depot and the tankers in the channel are all telling the same story: it has been a good summer.

stories.headline: Inside the depot's hiring push: why the Army's helicopter repair shop wants local mechanics
stories.dek: Corpus Christi Army Depot is recruiting helicopter mechanics this summer. The work is exacting, the hangars are hot and the jobs tend to last.
body: The short description of the work at Corpus Christi Army Depot is that it fixes helicopters. The long description takes a while.

The depot, on Naval Air Station Corpus Christi, is the Defense Department's primary depot for rotary-wing aircraft maintenance. Army helicopters arrive worn from years of flying, and the depot's civilian workforce takes them apart, inspects and repairs airframes, rebuilds engines and components and sends the aircraft back to units. This summer, the depot is hiring helicopter mechanics to keep that work moving.

"These are careers, not gigs," said Brenda Kowalczyk, a public affairs specialist for the depot. "People come in as mechanics and retire as mechanics, and in between they've touched aircraft that flew all over the world. There's a lot of pride in these hangars."

Kowalczyk said the depot looks for people with aviation maintenance training, military experience or industrial trade backgrounds, and it trains new hires on Army procedures and standards. The work is precise, documented and inspected at every step. "Everything gets checked, and then it gets checked again," she said. "That's the culture."
The hangars are also hot in August, and Kowalczyk did not pretend otherwise. "It's South Texas. Our folks hydrate, and they look out for each other," she said.

For the Coastal Bend, the depot's hiring matters beyond the base fence. Its civilian payroll ripples through Flour Bluff, the Southside and beyond, and the skills it builds, from sheet metal and hydraulics to wiring and avionics, are the kind that stay in a community.

The work also connects to readiness far from Texas. Helicopters rebuilt here go back into service with years of flying left in them, and the pace of that work affects how many aircraft Army units have available. That link is why depot hiring is about more than local jobs. For job seekers, it also means steady hours and federal benefits in a region where many skilled trades rise and fall with oil and construction.

The depot shares the air station with Navy flight training squadrons, which have flown a normal summer schedule, and with a Coast Guard air station. Openings are posted on USAJOBS, Kowalczyk said, and the depot encourages applicants who are new to aviation to apply if they have strong mechanical skills.

stories.headline: Before the heart of hurricane season, relief warehouses fill and freight firms sign on standby
stories.dek: Relief agencies are stocking shelves and freight forwarders are signing standby contracts so supplies can move quickly if a storm hits the Coastal Bend.
body: In warehouses around Corpus Christi this month, the shelves are filling: pallets of bottled water, tarps, cots, hygiene kits and nonperishable food, stacked, shrink-wrapped and waiting for a storm everyone hopes will not come.

Relief agencies are stocking their warehouses ahead of the peak of hurricane season, and freight forwarders that move supplies into disaster areas are signing standby relief contracts, agreements that let agencies call on trucks, containers and handling capacity on short notice.

"A standby contract is basically a reservation you hope you never use," said Terry Akins, regional manager for Gulf Relief Logistics, a freight forwarder that handles relief cargo through the Port of Corpus Christi. "We pre-plan the lanes, line up the boxes and the drivers, and if the call comes we're moving freight in hours, not days."

Akins said the work this time of year is mostly planning: confirming warehouse space, mapping alternate routes in case a highway or the port is closed, and deciding which supplies need to move first. "The stuff people need on day one is water, power and somewhere dry to sleep," he said. "If it's not staged before the storm, you're shipping it after, and after is always slower."

Neighborhood groups are stocking up, too. Pastor Gloria Whitfield, who runs a relief hub out of her church's fellowship hall in a low-income neighborhood near the bay, said her shelves are filling with canned goods, diapers and bottled water donated by members and neighbors. "The big trucks matter," Whitfield said. "But the first plate of food after a storm usually comes from somebody's church kitchen."
The port is a key link in that chain. In normal times it is busy with near-record crude exports. In a disaster, it is one of the ways bulk relief cargo can reach the region when highways are jammed.
Akins said the hardest part of standby work is that success is invisible. "If we did our job right," he said, "nobody ever hears my name."

stories.headline: Peak hurricane season is coming. Here's what to stock now
stories.dek: Relief agencies are filling their warehouses. Your household can do the same, a little at a time.
body: Relief agencies across the Coastal Bend are stocking warehouses ahead of the peak of hurricane season. Harborline 6 asked county emergency managers what families should have at home. The answer: more than you think, and sooner than you think.

"Buy a little every time you go to the store," says Dwayne Pruitt, public information officer for the Nueces County Office of Emergency Management. "If you wait for a forecast, so does everybody else, and the shelves are empty."

Your stock list: Water for every person and pet for several days. Nonperishable food that does not need cooking. A manual can opener. Prescription medicines and copies of prescriptions. Flashlights and extra batteries. A battery or hand-crank radio. Phone chargers and a power bank. Cash in small bills. A first-aid kit. Baby and pet supplies if you need them.
Paper matters: Keep IDs, insurance policies, leases and medical information in a waterproof bag. Take photos of them, and of your home's contents, on your phone.

Plan your exit: Know your evacuation zone. If you do not have a car, register for evacuation assistance by dialing 2-1-1. Pick an out-of-town contact for your family and make sure everyone has the number.
Help your neighbors: If you have room in your car, tell a neighbor who does not. Check on older residents and anyone who lives alone.
Do it in pieces: Add one or two items to every grocery run instead of buying everything at once. By the time the season peaks, your kit is done.

stories.headline: Church pantries stock up for storm season in neighborhoods that know the gaps
stories.dek: In low-income neighborhoods near the bay, church relief hubs are filling shelves now, because residents say help has to start close to home.
body: The fellowship hall at Pastor Gloria Whitfield's church is starting to look like a warehouse. Cases of bottled water line one wall. Canned beans, rice, diapers and baby wipes cover the folding tables. A whiteboard by the kitchen tracks what has come in and what is still needed.
"Batteries," Whitfield, 59, said, pointing at the board. "Everybody brings beans. Nobody brings batteries."

Relief agencies across the Coastal Bend are stocking warehouses ahead of the peak of hurricane season, and freight forwarders are signing standby relief contracts so larger shipments can move quickly. In neighborhoods near the bay, church and neighborhood hubs are doing their own version of the same work.

The reason is practical. Many households here do not have a car, and bus gaps already make it hard to reach a grocery store across town on an ordinary day, as Coastline Public Radio reported last month. Advocates say people without cars will turn first to places they can walk to.

The pattern is not unique to Corpus Christi. Disaster researchers have long noted that in neighborhoods with fewer cars and fewer resources, people tend to turn first to nearby institutions they already trust, such as churches, corner stores and community centers, especially in the first days after a disaster.

Rosa Elizondo, 38, a home health aide and mother of three who relies on buses, stopped by on a recent evening with her kids to help sort donations. "They help me all year. This is me helping back," Elizondo said, as her youngest stacked cans into a crooked tower. "Also, the air conditioning in here is better than mine. Don't tell her I said that."

Whitfield said she is not trying to replace county or federal relief, only to cover the hours or days before it arrives. "When the big trucks come, praise God," she said. "Until then, it's us. It has always been us first."

Her notebook of neighbors without cars or phones has grown this summer, she said, and she has been helping people register for evacuation assistance through the state's 2-1-1 registry.
