She wants county officials to see hubs like hers as partners. "We already know who needs what," she said. "Use us."

stories.headline: Editor's note: Don't let a calm summer fool you
stories.dek: The Coastal Bend has had a busy, sunny summer. That is exactly why base families should finish their hurricane prep now.
body: This is an opinion column from the editor of Anchor & Rotor Weekly.

It has been a good summer around here. The flight line has been busy with training, the depot is hiring, the island businesses are booming and a lot of us have spent our weekends on the beach. When things are this calm, it is easy to push the hurricane checklist to next week.

I have been a Navy spouse long enough to know how that goes. Next week becomes next month, and then one day the store is out of water and you are standing in the bread aisle with a toddler on your hip, wondering why you didn't do this in August.

So here is my pitch, from one family to another. Relief agencies are already stocking their warehouses for the peak of the season. Do the same at home, a little at a time. Nueces County is still urging residents without cars to register for evacuation help through 2-1-1. If your spouse is away and you share one car, think hard about whether that means you. And know your evacuation zone, which depends on where you live, not where you work.

Talk to your kids about the plan in a calm voice, on a calm day. Put the important papers in one waterproof bag. Make sure your command knows how to reach you if you leave town, and that you know how to check in.
And look out for the new families. Moving season brings people who have never lived on a coast. Invite them over, share your list and show them which aisle the batteries are in.
None of this is about fear. It is about getting the boring part done while the sun is shining, so that if a storm ever does come, we can spend our energy on each other instead of on the bread aisle.
Done your prep? Send us your best tip, and we will share the good ones in a future issue.

stories.headline: Perseids peak tonight, and Coastal Bend stargazers head for dark skies on the islands
stories.dek: The year's most popular meteor shower peaks overnight. The best views are away from city lights, and a Flour Bluff hobby astronomer has some advice.
body: If you are willing to stay up late and drive a little, the sky over the Coastal Bend has a show tonight. The Perseid meteor shower peaks overnight Thursday into Friday morning, and the best place to watch is somewhere dark: a stretch of beach on Padre or Mustang Island, well away from parking-lot lights and condo balconies.

The Perseids are bits of debris shed by a comet, and Earth passes through the trail every August. Under dark skies, patient watchers can see many meteors an hour near the peak, though moonlight, clouds and city glow cut that number down.

Jaime Ortega, 42, a Flour Bluff hobby astronomer who films the night sky, has been planning his Perseids night for weeks. He sets a camera on a tripod, aims it high and lets it run for hours. "Patience is the whole trick," Ortega said. "Lie down, look up, give your eyes 20 minutes to adjust and put your phone away. The phone ruins everything."

He has learned to read what shows up in his footage. "After a while you know what everything looks like," Ortega said. "A meteor is a quick streak. A satellite is a slow, steady dot. The planes from the air station blink and head home. Once you know the regulars, anything new jumps out at you."

Tips: Get away from city lights; the islands' darker beaches are a good bet. Bring a blanket or reclining chair, bug spray and water. Watch after midnight, when meteor rates usually climb. Scan the whole sky rather than staring at one spot. Respect beach rules and private property, and keep vehicles off the dunes.

Summer nights have been mostly clear lately, though a passing cloud bank can always spoil the view. The islands have been crowded all summer, so expect company. "That's part of it," Ortega said. "You hear a whole beach go 'Ooh' at the same time. Best sound in the world."

stories.headline: Corpus Christi crude loadings stay strong into August; offshore waits persist
stories.dek: Export terminals keep up a near-record pace as summer winds down; analysts see steady demand and a predictable loading rhythm.
body: CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Sabal Energy Wire) — Crude export loadings at the Port of Corpus Christi remained near record pace into mid-August, with tankers continuing to queue at the offshore anchorage east of Port Aransas for berth windows, market participants said.
The pace has held since early summer. Pipeline flows from the Permian Basin keep terminal tanks cycling, and charterers have kept tonnage positioned in the western Gulf to meet loading dates.

Terminal operators at Corpus Christi have added storage and dock capacity in recent years, and a deeper channel lets larger tankers load more crude per call. Freight market participants said the steady rhythm of loadings has helped charterers plan cargoes weeks ahead.

"Nothing about this summer has surprised us, which in this market is a compliment," said Grace Holloway, an energy market analyst at Lanternfish Energy Analytics. "Barrels in, barrels out, ships waiting their turn. The machine is doing exactly what it was built to do."

Holloway said that predictability has its own value. "Buyers plan around Corpus because the dates hold, and they pay for that certainty in ways that never show up on an invoice," she said. "Reliability is a product too."

Late summer also brings a planned military movement through the port, as a Fort Hood aviation brigade ships its helicopters and equipment for an overseas rotation. Port officials have said military cargo will be handled alongside regular business, and the equipment is expected to move over general cargo berths rather than crude docks.
Sabal Energy Wire will continue weekly coverage of Gulf Coast export flows.

stories.headline: Rosa Elizondo's hurricane plan runs on bus time and neighbors
stories.dek: A home health aide and mother of three, Elizondo has spent the summer piecing together a plan for a storm she hopes never comes. It starts with not having a car.
body: On Saturday mornings, Rosa Elizondo makes pancakes, and her three kids argue about who gets the first one. Her youngest, 6, usually wins. Her oldest, a teenager, usually pretends not to care.

The rest of the week, Elizondo, 38, belongs to the bus. A home health aide, she rides city buses between clients' homes across Corpus Christi, packing frozen water bottles against the heat and keeping a mental map of every route, every transfer and every stop with decent shade. She rents a duplex a few blocks from the bay, in one of the low-income neighborhoods where many families do not have a car.
This summer, between shifts, she has been working on another kind of map: what she would do if a hurricane came.

It started at a Nueces County preparedness fair last month, where, as the Ledger reported, county emergency managers urged residents without cars to register for evacuation assistance. Elizondo left with a registration card and a free flashlight. Since then, she has talked the question through with her pastor, her neighbors and her kids.

"Everybody's plan says 'drive,'" she said. "So my plan is a list of people who drive." Her list includes a neighbor, friends from church and Pastor Gloria Whitfield, who runs a relief hub from her church's fellowship hall and keeps a notebook of neighbors without cars. "And the county, if they come," she added. "I pray they come."

Advocates in neighborhoods near the bay have been pushing for more evacuation rides, saying the bus gaps that strand families on ordinary weekends would be worse in an emergency. Elizondo is blunter. "On a normal Sunday, the bus takes forever," she said. "On a storm day? Nobody's going to stand at a bus stop in the rain with three kids. I'm not going to."

She has packed a bag, more or less: documents in a zipper bag, a change of clothes for everybody, a phone charger and whatever medicine the kids might need. The flashlight from the fair is in there too, though her youngest keeps borrowing it.
Asked whether she worries, Elizondo laughed. "Ay, mija, I'm a mom. I worry about everything," she said. "But I'd rather worry now, while it's sunny, than later."

stories.headline: Summer traffic crowds the Port Aransas pass as tankers, ferries and charters share the entrance
stories.dek: Deep-draft crude traffic and a strong tourist season are packing the entrance channel at Port Aransas this August.
body: The entrance channel between the jetties at Port Aransas is carrying a heavy mix of traffic this summer, with crude tankers moving at a near-record export pace alongside ferries, charter boats and recreational vessels drawn by a strong tourist season.

Deep draft: Laden tankers outbound from Corpus Christi terminals and ballast tankers inbound from the offshore anchorage transit the pass with pilots aboard and tug escort as required. Large vessels have limited room to maneuver in the confined entrance and depend on other traffic to keep clear.

Ferries: The state-run ferries between Harbor Island and Port Aransas cross the ship channel just inside the pass, and summer demand keeps them running almost constantly. Ferry crossings are timed around deep-draft movements.

Small craft: Port Aransas businesses report a strong summer, with charters and bait shops busy. Charter boats, bay boats, kayaks and personal watercraft add to congestion around the jetties, particularly on weekend mornings and late afternoons. Anglers on the jetty rocks and boats anchored near the pass are a familiar sight to pilots bringing ships through.

Tugs and support: Harbor tugs, pilot boats and offshore supply vessels round out the picture. Tug crews working the entrance spend much of the summer threading between pleasure boats on their way to and from assignments.
Wind and visibility: Afternoon sea breezes and summer squalls can raise a steep chop in the pass and briefly cut visibility, adding to the workload for pilots and small-boat operators alike.

Rules of the road: Recreational boaters must not impede vessels that can navigate safely only within the channel, and federal navigation rules apply throughout the pass. The Coast Guard oversees channel traffic and can impose safety measures when conditions require.
Gulfwater will continue to track entrance-channel and anchorage conditions as the season moves toward its late-summer peak.
